% DRIFT formal specification -- the metabolic bridge's scaling law.
%
% The source of truth is DRIFT's code:
%   drift/metabolic.py :: MetabolicBridge.get_constraints_with_scalings
%       basal = map_config.get("basal_scaling", 0.1)
%       max_s = map_config.get("max_scaling", 0.9)
%       positive influence: scaling = basal + max_s * protein_level
%       negative influence: scaling = (basal + max_s) - max_s * protein_level
%
% The machine-checkable block below is GENERATED by
%   python3 scripts/export_drift_to_qed.py --spec-sync
% and is verified by

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
% THEOREM 1 (the two branches split one budget).  For every protein level,
%     basal + max*protein + max*(1 - protein) = basal + max.
%
% THEOREM 2 (complementarity).  For every protein level,
%     (basal + max) - max*protein = basal + max*(1 - protein),
% i.e. the negative-influence branch is the complement of the positive one.
%
% THEOREM 3 (branch symmetry).  For every protein level, the positive and
% negative branches are symmetric about the midpoint of the budget:
%     (basal + max*protein) + ((basal + max) - max*protein)
%         = basal + (basal + max).
% Their sum is constant in protein_level, so moving protein level up
% raises one branch by exactly what it lowers the other.  This is not a
% bounds theorem: the interval bound 0.1 <= scaling <= 1.0 needs the
% premise 0 <= protein_level <= 1, which the statement language cannot
% express.  The numeric bounds are a code-level invariant, held by the
% unit test in tests/test_scientific_rigor.py (the bridge clamps the
% protein level into [0, 1] before scaling).  What the block certifies is
% the algebra: the two branches split one budget, the negative branch is
% the complement of the positive one, and their sum is constant.
%
% THE CONSTANTS ARE SCALED.  The statement language has NO decimal
% literal -- "0.1" does not tokenize, and a statement carrying one fails
% closed and is never proved (measured: the first export of this file
% failed on exactly that).  The exporter therefore multiplies the identity
% through by 10, the smallest scale that makes both constants integral, and
% emits the scaled identity: "1 + 9 * protein_level + 9 * (1 - protein_level)
% = 1 + 9" is "0.1 + 0.9 * protein_level + 0.9 * (1 - protein_level) =
% 0.1 + 0.9" times ten.  Divide by the scale to read the shipped values.
%% QED-BEGIN
%% QED 1 + 9 * protein_level + 9 * (1 - protein_level) = 1 + 9
%% QED (1 + 9) - 9 * protein_level = 1 + 9 * (1 - protein_level)
%% QED (1 + 9 * protein_level) + ((1 + 9) - 9 * protein_level) = 1 + (1 + 9)
%% QED-END
